paragraphs.source_en: Traditionally, this stylistic group was thought to represent the earliest rock art phase in the Central Sahara, preceding the appearance of domestic stock represented later in the Pastoral style. The Bubaline style was proposed to date to the Early Holocene or even to the Late Pleistocene (Mori 1974; 2000). This was principally based on a dark patina which was found to cover the engravings, which is known to have formed during the Early and Middle Holocene (Zerboni 2008). However, recent survey has shown that mixed with the fully patinated wild animals of the Bubaline style there are several engravings of clearly domesticated cattle (because they are adorned with pendants and collars and are depicted with deformed horns which are typical for domestic cattle and also cattle which are led by men) showing the same dark patina (Muzzolini 1995a, b; Jelinek 2004).

paragraphs.source_en: Also the wild animals represented are not an indicator of a great antiquity as the Bubalus antiquus became extinct relatively late, at around 5,000 BP (Barnett & Mattingly 2003) and hippo bones found in the Ténéré were dated to 3,500 BP (Le Quellec 2006b). Thus scholars have divided opinions into those who still defend a very ancient age for these engravings and those who claim that they all were created in the Pastoral phase which started at around 7,500 BP.

paragraphs.source_en: The Bubaline engravings are located on rock walls in the open, where there is very little hope of finding a connection between the art and datable stratified deposits (Mori 1974). Wadi Djerat in the northern Tassili has one of the greatest accumulations of the Bubaline engravings. It was noticed that Levallois-type tools, typical for Aterian industries, are present on the edges of the wadi and practically nowhere else, which led to the hypothesis that Bubaline engravings might have been the work of Late Pleistocene Aterian populations probably present in the region before 20,000 BP (Lhote 1976; Hachid 1998; Aumassip 2004).
